newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. seeks Asian, Latam shift for financial pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks Asian, Latam shift for financial pact.

text.p: The United States promised on Thursday it would next month offer a major opening of its financial services markets in a bid to get a World Trade Organisation (WTO) pact by the end of the year.

But a senior U.S. trade official said key Asian and Latin American countries would have to pledge to lift a range of current restrictions on foreign firms in the sector before Washington could sign up to a deal.

The official was speaking after a meeting of a WTO group involving the more than 40 countries in the negotiations, which were resumed in April after an earlier effort to shape a global accord failed last year due to U.S. objections.
The official said the U.S. package would be tabled by July 14, the date agreed by most participants in the talks, which cover banking, securities and insurance operations.

"For our offer to be turned into actual commitments in the WTO at the end of this negotiation, we will need to see meaningful market opening offers from a wide range of countries," the official added.
These would have to provide "substantially full national treatment" -- or guarantees that foreign firms would be treated in the same way as domestic companies -- and "market access".

The offers would have to be significantly better than those tabled in the earlier talks by "a wide range of participants, but specifically the key emerging markets from Latin America and Asia," the official said.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, declined to say which countries the United States had in mind but diplomats said Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Malaysia, South Korea, Thailand and Philippines were among them.

All of these signed up to an interim agreement stitched together by the European Union -- which on Thursday also promised it would make a new offer by July 14 -- when the United States pulled out at the end of June last year.
That accord, which in many cases only froze minimal terms for the operation of foreign firms currently set by a range of emerging economies, is due to run out by the end of the year.

At the WTO's first Ministerial Conference in Singapore last December, officials from the now 131 members of the trade body agreed to resume the bid for a global deal and set a deadline of December 12 this year for its completion.

Since then, the big four trade powers -- the United States, the EU, Japan and Canada -- and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC), which includes many developing countries, have renewed their commitment to reaching a deal.

Diplomats also hope that a WTO pact concluded in February to liberalise global telecommunications will provide a psychological boost for a financial services pact, which would involve many of the same countries.
Trade diplomats said other countries which promised new offers on the table by the middle of next month included Japan, Canada, Australia, Hong Kong, Bahrain and Switzerland.
But although several developing countries -- including Egypt, Thailand and Chile -- who spoke said they wanted to see an accord, they avoided pledging to meet the July 14 date.

The diplomats said Pakistan urged the need for "flexibility" in any accord -- a reference to the demand from emerging economies for a phased implementation of liberalisation measures to allow their domestic financial industries to adjust.
